target.title: Non-Audible Murmur (NAM) Recognition
target.venue: IEICE Transactions on Information and Systems, Vol. E89-D, No. 1

read.pdf: Figs. 1-9 and Table 1; visually checked all figures and the complete result table against the published PDF

entries.text: The authors propose a practical speech-input interface that recognizes non-audible murmur (NAM) through body-transmitted sound rather than an external microphone.
entries.condition: Proposed interface; feasibility tested with a stethoscopic skin-contact microphone and Japanese speech recognizer.
entries.quote:
We propose a new practical input interface for the recog-
nition of Non-Audible Murmur (NAM), which is defined as articulated res-
piratory sound without vocal-fold vibration transmitted through the soft tis-
sues of the head.

entries.text: The authors introduce and define NAM as articulated respiratory sound without vocal-fold vibration, transmitted through soft tissues of the head.
entries.condition: Conceptual definition; the authors note that NAM and whisper speech have a vague acoustic boundary.

entries.text: NAM is presented as a previously unused communication/input channel and a possible second-voice interface for human-machine and human-human communication.
entries.condition: Proposed use, not a reported end-to-end communication trial.

entries.text: The authors state that NAM can be performed easily without acquiring a new skill.
entries.condition: General statement about the utterance action; not tested as a user-learning outcome.

entries.text: The proposed recognition system retains existing speech-recognition technology and replaces the ordinary-speech acoustic model with a NAM acoustic model.
entries.condition: HMM recognition architecture; the paper describes acoustic-model replacement as the principal system change.

entries.text: The authors characterize the technique's distinguishing features as inaudible utterance, direct sensing at the body surface, and robustness to noise.
entries.condition: Authors' stated distinctions; noise robustness is qualified by the incomplete microphone soundproofing and lower B-D scores.
entries.quote: body directly’ and ‘robustness against noise.”

entries.text: The conceptual interface allows recognized parameters such as text to be visually checked after recognition.
entries.condition: Conceptual workflow only; no confirmation behavior or user study is reported.

entries.text: The conceptual interface allows a user to correct recognized text in some cases.
entries.condition: Correction is mentioned as a possible step; no correction method or evaluation is described.

entries.text: The authors project NAM recognition as a future hands-free input device for portable or wearable terminals, potentially replacing a keyboard or numeric keypad.
entries.condition: Future projection; no deployed or longitudinal system is evaluated.

entries.text: The authors suggest NAM recognition might assist people unable to speak with a normal voice.
entries.condition: Prospective application; the experiment reports a male speaker and no vocally impaired participants.

entries.text: The authors built a skin-adhering stethoscopic NAM microphone by inserting a small condenser microphone into a medical stethoscope tube.
entries.condition: Sensor acquisition; microphone mounted on skin to capture flesh-transmitted vibration.
entries.quote: and implanted a small condenser microphone into it for the

entries.text: The authors identify the optimal microphone location as just covering the lower part of the mastoid process behind the ear.
entries.condition: Selected after comparing attachment locations; the position is described anatomically, without standardized placement coordinates.

entries.text: The microphone frequency response has a peak of about 15 dB around 4-6 kHz.
entries.condition: Stethoscopic microphone frequency response; paper attributes the peak to the stethoscopic structure and suction disk.

entries.text: Figure 4 reports sensitivity/SNR of -46.43/56.92 without the plate and -54.34/49.01 with the plate.
entries.condition: Microphone frequency-response figure's plate comparison; values visually transcribed from Fig. 4.

entries.text: The microphone's polyester fixing board is 40 mm in diameter.
entries.condition: Physical specification of the hand-made stethoscopic microphone fixation plate.

entries.text: The authors report that the microphone remained attached to skin for 24 hours without coming off.
entries.condition: Wear observation described for the device; not a deployment study.

entries.text: NAM samples were recorded at 16 kHz with 16-bit digitization.
entries.condition: Training and evaluation recording setup using microphone amplifier and computer with Linux/ALSA.

entries.text: The authors selected additional EM re-estimation of a speaker-independent normal-speech model as their first NAM-modeling approach; they list NAM-only training and MLLR adaptation as alternatives.
entries.condition: NAM recognition training; chosen approach uses numerous NAM samples to retrain the normal-speech model.

entries.text: The authors concede that a precise acoustic/physical boundary between NAM and whisper speech is difficult to define.
entries.condition: Conceptual distinction; NAM varies from quiet exhalation with articulation to sounds approaching whisper voice.
entries.quote:
It is difficult to define precisely the acoustic differ-
ences and physical borderline between “NAM speech” and
“whisper speech”, which is voiceless sound using a turbu-
lent flow (white noise) by narrowing the glottis as a sound
source.

entries.text: The authors note that breathless lip-sync-like NAM can be inconvenient: long sentences cannot be uttered and utterance on/off cannot be discriminated.
entries.condition: Applies to utterance actions with no expiration; not the breath-supported NAM condition used for the recognition experiment.

entries.text: At earlier jaw/neck attachment positions, consonant-vowel balance and other acoustic issues prevented the authors from obtaining a recognition rate they considered numerically evaluable.
entries.condition: Exploratory sensor-position trials before selecting the location near the mastoid process.

entries.text: Available earphone-type bone-conduction microphones produced too small a NAM signal for a good S/N ratio, although they sampled normal speech comparatively clearly.
entries.condition: Authors' comparison with commercially available bone-conduction microphones; no quantitative recognition results reported for those devices.

entries.text: The authors report NAM spectral content only up to about the second formant below 2 kHz, attributing the loss of higher formants to soft-tissue low-pass filtering and microphone placement.
entries.condition: Acoustic characterization of NAM through the stethoscopic microphone.

entries.text: The authors state that more NAM-specialized acoustic models require more time and effort for data collection and operation.
entries.condition: Comparison among NAM-only modeling, additional-EM retraining, and lower-data MLLR adaptation strategies.

questions.q: What quantitative performance does the paper actually report, and how does the noisy-condition result compare with its robustness claim?
questions.answer: Table 1 reports word-recognition accuracy of 93.3% in quiet, 90.0% with classical music, 89.2% with NHK TV news, and 88.4% in the clinic/office-like condition (24 sentences per condition). The authors describe B-D as around 90%, while also conceding that incomplete microphone soundproofing and body-transmitted noise reduced performance.

questions.q: Does the evaluation establish generalization to new speakers or to the intended assistive population?
questions.answer: No. Training samples are described for a male speaker, results use a speaker-dependent model, and the paper does not specify evaluation-speaker count or train/test speaker overlap. Vocally impaired users are proposed as a future application, not evaluated.

questions.q: Can the reported test be confirmed as independent of training and selection data?
questions.answer: The paper reports 24 Mainichi evaluation sentences and 1,255 Mainichi/JNAS training sentences, but gives no sentence-level exclusion/split description or separate validation/selection set.

questions.q: Were online confirmation, correction, or deployment evaluated?
questions.answer: No. Visual checking/correction and future wearable/communication applications are proposed conceptually; the reported result is offline recognition, with no interaction or deployment evaluation.

questions.q: Is the 2006 English paper a version of the 2004 Japanese IEICE D-II paper (same Table 1)?
questions.answer: Yes: the English paper sits in the 2004 IEICE Excellent Paper Award special section and the Japanese Table 1 row A is identical; first public set to 2004-09.

questions.q: Do rows A-C of Table 1 match the group's ICASSP 2003 table, and what training data did that model use?
questions.answer: Yes, to rounding (93.61/93.33, 91.11/90.00, 89.72/89.17); the 2003 model was trained on 2,100 ATR files only, from the same male speaker.

questions.q: Was an air-microphone baseline in the same everyday-noise conditions reported by the group around the same time?
questions.answer: Yes, EUSIPCO 2004: close-talking 94.4/91.7/91.9 vs NAM microphone 93.8/93.2/92.9 for audible speech (quiet/TV news/music).

questions.q: What does NAM recognition score with noise physically present at stated levels?
questions.answer: Heracleous et al. 2007: 83.7% clean, 66.9% at 50 dBA, 53.3% at 60 dBA (four noises, female speaker).
